title: Baruch
subtitle: a scribe's book for exiles: confession, wisdom, a mother's comfort, and a letter against idols
lead: Baruch is a short book found in the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint). It is set among the Jews taken to Babylon. It opens by saying that Baruch, the scribe of the prophet Jeremiah, wrote it in Babylon in the fifth year after the Chaldeans burned Jerusalem, and read it aloud to King Jeconiah and the exiles (1:1–4). It holds four different pieces. First comes a prose frame in which the exiles send money and a book to Jerusalem (1:1–14). Next is a long confession of the nation's sins, close in wording to Daniel's prayer (1:15–3:8). Then a poem asks where wisdom can be found and answers that God gave it to Israel as the Law (3:9–4:4). Last, Jerusalem speaks as a mother to her exiled children, and is then told to look east and see them coming home (4:5–5:9).

Chapter 6 is a separate work, the Letter of Jeremiah, written in Jeremiah's name to Jews about to be carried to Babylon. It mocks the gilded gods carried in Babylon's processions, item by item, and ends round after round with a refrain: they are not gods, so have no fear of them. Greek manuscripts place it as its own book after Lamentations (Adams), and the Orthodox Study Bible lists it as its own book. The Latin Vulgate, the Douay-Rheims and the King James Version print it as Baruch's sixth chapter. This site follows that numbering but treats the Letter as its own work throughout.

Who reads it as Scripture. The Catholic Church counts Baruch, with the Letter as its chapter 6, among the deuterocanonical books. The Orthodox churches read Baruch and the Letter as two books of their Old Testament, and the Ethiopian Orthodox Church counts Baruch too. Anglicans and Lutherans place them among the Apocrypha, books read for example of life but not to establish doctrine. The Reformed and Baptist confessions do not count them as Scripture, and they are not in the Jewish Bible. Jeremiah's book page asks the question side by side for each church ("Are Baruch and the Letter of Jeremiah part of the Bible?"); this page does not repeat it. Scholars disagree about almost everything else: who wrote the pieces, when, and in what language. The proposals for Baruch run from the 500s BC to after AD 70. For the Letter they run from Jeremiah's own day to the last centuries BC.
facts: The Catholic Church ("Jeremias, with Baruch" in the list of the Council of Trent, 1546; Baruch is in the Catechism's list, 120), the Eastern Orthodox churches (Baruch and the Letter as two books), and the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church (Baruch in the narrower list of its canon, the Letter inside a longer book of Jeremiah's). Among the Apocrypha for Anglicans ("Baruch the Prophet," Article VI) and Lutherans. Not Scripture in the Reformed and Baptist confessions, or for Judaism.

Baruch 1–5 names Baruch son of Neriah, Jeremiah's scribe (1:1). Catholic scholars of the early 1900s defended his authorship, and those who saw earlier pieces in the book held that he compiled them (Gigot). Critical scholars generally think two or three unknown Jewish writers composed the parts and an editor joined them, long after Baruch (Whitehouse; Toy; Gigot reports the same of the critics of his day). The Letter's title names Jeremiah (6:1). Gigot reports that most critics of his day denied that Jeremiah wrote it, and that Jerome called it pseudepigraphos, a writing under a borrowed name.

Baruch: disputed. The book's own date is the fifth year after the fall of Jerusalem, about 582 BC (1:2). Scholars have proposed the Persian period (Ewald), the 100s BC (Toy), before 100 BC (Harwell) and after AD 70 (Kneucker, Schürer, Whitehouse). Irenaeus quoted it as Jeremiah's words late in the 100s AD. The Letter: Adams puts a Hebrew original, if there was one, between the 500s and the first century BC. C. J. Ball read its "seven generations" (6:2) as a clue to about 317–306 BC. The Greek of the Letter was made after Alexander's conquests, likely in the 200s or 100s BC (Adams).
Babylon, among the exiles of Jeconiah's deportation, by the river Sud (1:4), with a book and money sent to Jerusalem (1:7–14). The Letter is addressed to Jews about to be led away to Babylon (6:1).
Unknown. Proposals include Judea, Babylonia, Egypt and the wider dispersion; for the Letter, Egypt (Alexandria), Babylon and Palestine have all been suggested (Adams).

Disputed. Whitehouse wrote in 1913 that nearly all living scholars held the prose (1:1–3:8) was composed in Hebrew. The poems are argued both ways, and some older critics, such as Grotius and Eichhorn, thought the whole book was Greek (Whitehouse). For the Letter, most scholars of the 1900s argued for a lost Hebrew original, and some recent scholars read it as Greek composition (Adams; VanderKam).

Greek: Codex Vaticanus (300s AD, the text Swete prints), Alexandrinus (400s), Marchalianus (500s) and Venetus, with later minuscules. Codex Sinaiticus has neither work (Whitehouse); Adams thinks they were in a part of it now lost after Lamentations 2:20. A tiny Greek papyrus from Qumran Cave 7 (7Q2) is thought to hold part of the Letter. Ancient versions: Syriac (including the Syro-Hexapla, made from Origen's Greek in the 600s), Old Latin (taken into the Vulgate), Coptic, Ethiopic, Arabic and Armenian. No Hebrew copy survives of either work.

Baruch: a prose narrative frame, a national confession and prayer, a wisdom poem and a poem of lament and consolation. The Letter: a sermon against idols in the form of a letter, with a repeated refrain.
6 chapters, 213 verses: Baruch 1–5 (141 verses) and the Letter of Jeremiah (chapter 6, 72 verses), in the numbering of Swete's Greek text
authorship: Baruch son of Neriah wrote Baruch 1–5 in Babylon, as 1:1 says, and Jeremiah wrote the Letter. Early Christian writers often quoted Baruch as the words of Jeremiah himself: Irenaeus quotes 4:36–5:9 as what "Jeremiah the prophet has pointed out" (Against Heresies 5.35.1), and Cyprian quotes 3:36–38 under Jeremiah's name (Testimonies 2.6). Francis Gigot's article in the Catholic Encyclopedia (1907) defended Baruch's authorship and allowed that he may have joined several earlier documents; it argued that an inspired editor would leave the book inspired either way.

Critical scholars since the 1800s have generally seen two or three pieces from different hands (Whitehouse; Gigot reports that "contemporary critics generally" see a compilation). The prose of 1:1–3:8 draws whole clauses from Daniel 9 and much from Jeremiah and Deuteronomy; the wisdom poem draws on Job 28, Proverbs 8 and Sirach 24; the last poem draws on Isaiah 40–66 and is very close to Psalms of Solomon 11 (Whitehouse; Toy). An editor, perhaps the writer of the prose, joined them and set them in Baruch's name (Harwell). C. H. Toy wrote in 1902 that "very few scholars" still held that Jeremiah's secretary wrote it.

The Letter is a separate work: it has its own title and its own subject. Gigot, a Catholic scholar, called it "truly distinct from the rest of the work." Gigot reports that Jerome called it pseudepigraphos, a writing under a borrowed name. C. J. Ball found its picture of Babylonian worship true to what is known of Babylonian religion, and took its author for a Jew of the eastern dispersion writing to keep waverers from the temples. Adams notes that the idea of a letter from Jeremiah comes from the real letter of Jeremiah 29, and that the Letter is closely tied to Jeremiah 10.

audience.to: Jews living under foreign rule, whether in the dispersion or in a Judea that felt itself still in exile, centuries after the Babylonian captivity. The book is set among the exiles of the 500s BC, but its frame asks for it to be read out "in the Lord's house" on feast days (1:14), so it was written to be heard by a gathered community. Whether Jews ever read it in worship is uncertain. The Apostolic Constitutions, a Christian work of about AD 380, say that Jews read Lamentations and Baruch on the tenth day of the month Gorpiaeus. C. H. Toy took the month to be probably Ab, but he judged the report "can hardly be considered authoritative" and, if true, true only of "some group of Hellenistic Jews." Toy also wrote that the Alexandrian Jews accepted the book "as a work of edification." The Letter is written to people who live among idol worship and are tempted to fear it (6:4–5).
audience.why: To give exiles words to pray and reasons to hope. The confession teaches them to say that God is just and the shame is theirs (1:15–2:10), and to ask mercy for his name's sake (2:11–3:8). The wisdom poem tells them why they are in a foreign land, because they left the fountain of wisdom (3:10–12), and where life is to be found: in the book of God's commands, which belongs to Israel (4:1–4). The mother's poem gives them Jerusalem's own voice, grieving and then comforted, and promises their return (4:5–5:9). The Letter answers a daily temptation: the splendid gods of a powerful empire, carried shoulder-high through the streets, are wood and metal and cannot save. Knowing the readers changes the reading. Baruch is not a report about Baruch; it is words for an assembly (1:14) of a people who keep asking why they are still scattered, and the Letter is a sermon for people surrounded by other people's gods.
views: Exiles in Babylon (the book's own setting)

Read as it presents itself, Baruch was sent from Babylon to Jerusalem about 582 BC, and the Letter went to the captives of Jeconiah's deportation. Francis Gigot (1907) set out the Catholic case for Baruch's authorship, and said the book would still be inspired if a later inspired editor had joined its pieces.

C. H. Toy thought an editor of the Maccabean period joined the confession, which borrows from Daniel, to the frame, and placed the wisdom poem in the early Maccabean period. On this view the first readers were Judeans under the Seleucid kings, still waiting for the scattered to come home.
After the Temple's fall in AD 70

Kneucker, Schürer and O. C. Whitehouse read Nebuchadnezzar and his son Belshazzar (1:11–12) as a mask for Vespasian and his son Titus, and the burning of the Temple (1:2; 2:26) as the burning of AD 70. On this view the first readers were Jews who had to live under Rome after the catastrophe; Whitehouse suggested the circle of Johanan ben Zakkai. Gigot answered that Catholics easily disprove this date, and Harwell argued that Irenaeus's use of it as part of Jeremiah points earlier.

Whatever the date of the Hebrew pieces, the Greek book reached Jews who read the Greek Jeremiah. Thackeray showed that the prose of Baruch 1–2 and the later chapters of Greek Jeremiah were translated by one hand; Harwell extended this to the whole book, on the ground that all of it was written in Hebrew. Ball thought the Letter was passed among Jews living beside Babylonian worship, to keep the wavering from it.

outline: Baruch writes a book in Babylon and reads it to Jeconiah and the exiles; they weep, fast and collect money
The letter to Jerusalem: offer sacrifices, pray for Nebuchadnezzar and Belshazzar, read this book on the feast days
The confession: justice belongs to the Lord, shame to us; we did not listen
The prayer for mercy: remember your people, as you promised through Moses and the prophets
The wisdom poem: Israel in exile for leaving the fountain of wisdom; no one found her but God, who gave her to Jacob as the book of his commands
Jerusalem speaks as a mother to her exiled children: take courage
Jerusalem comforted: look east, take off your mourning, God is bringing your children home
The Letter of Jeremiah: the title, seven generations in Babylon, gods carried on shoulders, do not fear them
Round after round against the idols: their tongues, their clothes, their priests, their helplessness, each ending in the refrain that they are not gods

lenses.name: Catholic
lenses.desc: The Catholic Church counts Baruch, with the Letter of Jeremiah as its chapter 6, among the deuterocanonical books. The Council of Trent (1546) listed "Jeremias, with Baruch" as sacred and canonical, and the Easter Vigil has Baruch's wisdom poem (3:9–15, 32–4:4) as its sixth reading.

lenses.name: Orthodox
lenses.desc: The Orthodox churches read Baruch and the Letter of Jeremiah as two books, set with Jeremiah and Lamentations (Orthodox Study Bible). Athanasius and Cyril of Jerusalem counted both with Jeremiah among the canonical books, and Orthodox worship reads Baruch under Jeremiah's name on the eve of the Nativity.

lenses.name: Protestant
lenses.desc: Protestants place Baruch and the Letter among the Apocrypha. Article VI names "Baruch the Prophet" among the books read "for example of life" but not "to establish any doctrine," and Luther's Bible printed Baruch among the Apocrypha, books "not held equal to Holy Scripture, and yet useful and good to read" (in English). The Reformed and Baptist confessions give them no authority.

lenses.name: Historical-critical
lenses.desc: Critical scholars (Whitehouse, Toy, Harwell) read Baruch as a collection of pieces by different hands, built from Daniel, Jeremiah, Deuteronomy, Job, Isaiah and the wisdom books and set in Baruch's name, and the Letter as a separate Jewish sermon against idols in Jeremiah's name. Their dates and original languages are debated.

lenses.name: Jewish reception
lenses.desc: Neither work is in the Jewish Bible, and Jerome says the Hebrews of his day did not read Baruch. A Christian source, the Apostolic Constitutions, says some Jews read it with Lamentations on one day of the year, which Toy doubted. Rabbinic tradition remembers Baruch in Babylon as Ezra's teacher (Megillah 16b).

sections.b:
Read it as a book of four voices, put in the mouth of a scribe in exile. First the narrator, who sets the scene in Babylon and sends the book to Jerusalem with money and a request: pray for the king, and read this book aloud on the feast days (1:1–14). Then the people, who confess as one: the Lord is in the right, and we are ashamed (1:15–3:8). Then a wisdom teacher, who asks where understanding lives and answers that God found it and gave it to Israel as the book of his commands (3:9–4:4). Last, Jerusalem herself, a widowed mother who sent her children away weeping and is told to put on the robe of glory and watch them come home (4:5–5:9).

The movement is the point. The book goes from the past (why the exile happened) to the present (what to hold on to) to the future (the return). It follows the pattern of Deuteronomy 28–30: sin, curse, exile, turning back to God, and return to the land, which the prayer quotes almost word for word (2:29–35).

Then read chapter 6 as a different piece. The Letter of Jeremiah has its own title, its own audience and its own subject. Its humor is deliberate. Its writer piles up the gods' indignities, from the dust on their faces to the cats on their heads, and closes round after round with nearly the same words, so the hearers say the refrain with him.

The Plain English Translation follows the Greek of H. B. Swete's Old Testament in Greek (vol. 3, 1912), which prints Codex Vaticanus and gives the other great codices in its notes. Where the Plain English Translation follows another witness, a variant entry says so. The King James Apocrypha, the Latin Vulgate and the Douay-Rheims made from it are used to check sense only. No Hebrew text of either work survives, so every Hebraism or proposed Hebrew original mentioned on these pages is a scholar's reconstruction, labeled as such.

Verse numbers. This site keys every verse to Swete's numbering. The King James Version numbers some verses one lower: its 3:35–37 are this site's 3:36–38, and in chapter 6 the KJV makes the title a verse of its own, so its 6:2–73 are this site's 6:1–72. When you compare a KJV verse with this site, check the words, not only the number. The Orthodox reading "Baruch 3:35–4:4" on the eve of the Nativity is this site's 3:36–4:4.

Names. The Plain English Translation uses the forms English Bibles use (Jeconiah, Nebuchadnezzar, Belshazzar, Joakim), with the Greek in a note where it differs.

The confession (1:15–3:8). Its first part follows Daniel's prayer (Daniel 9:4–19) so closely that many clauses match, starting with "to us belongs the shame of our faces" (compare Daniel 9:7). C. H. Toy and O. C. Whitehouse thought Baruch borrows from Daniel; Whitehouse's reason is that Baruch's version is longer and repeats itself more. Ewald thought the borrowing went the other way. The prayer also weaves in Jeremiah (the yoke of the king of Babylon, Jeremiah 27:11–12; the voice of the bride and groom silenced, Jeremiah 7:34) and Deuteronomy 28–30.

The wisdom poem (3:9–4:4). It asks Job's question, "But wisdom: where can it be found?" (Job 28:12), answers in the language of Proverbs 8 and Deuteronomy 30:12–13, and draws on Sirach 24, where wisdom makes her home in Israel (Whitehouse). It is the clearest place in the book where wisdom and the Law become one (4:1).

The mother's poem (4:5–5:9). Jerusalem's voice comes from Lamentations 1 and Isaiah 49 and 54; the comfort comes from Isaiah 40 and 60. Its last verses run very close to Psalms of Solomon 11, line for line (Whitehouse prints the two side by side). Whitehouse held that Baruch borrowed from the psalm; R. H. Charles, his editor, thought both adapted one older Hebrew psalm; Harwell judged that the shared ideas were common stock since Second Isaiah and settle nothing.

Greek manuscripts place the Letter at the end of Jeremiah's books, after Lamentations, which follows Baruch (Adams). Latin Bibles attached it to Baruch as a sixth chapter (Adams), and the Douay-Rheims and the King James Version follow the Latin. In the Ethiopian Bible it is "the epistle to the captives," counted as chapter 6 of a longer book of Jeremiah's lamentations, which goes on with a prophecy against Pashhur and the story called 4 Baruch (Cowley).

Its model is Jeremiah's real letter to the exiles, "the letter that the prophet Jeremiah sent from Jerusalem" (Jeremiah 29:1), and Jeremiah's satire on idols in Jeremiah 10:1–16: the scarecrow in the cucumber field (6:69) is the picture of Jeremiah 10:5 in the Hebrew text, which the Greek of Jeremiah lacks (Adams). 2 Maccabees knows a tradition that Jeremiah warned the deported "not to let their minds be led astray when they saw images of gold and silver and the finery on them" (2 Maccabees 2:2); whether that is this Letter is debated.

Its picture of Babylon is concrete: gods carried in procession, priests who take the offerings, lamps, the women in the streets (6:43). C. J. Ball found these details true to what is known of Babylonian religion, and thought the writer knew Babylon in its decline, around 300 BC. Its claim of "seven generations" in Babylon (6:2), instead of Jeremiah's seventy years (Jeremiah 29:10), may be the writer's way of speaking to his own time; the Syriac version changes it to seventy years (Ball). Sean Adams notes that a small Greek papyrus from Qumran Cave 7, 7Q2, is thought to hold verses 43–44, though it has only twenty-two letters and the identification is not certain; if it is the Letter, it is the oldest copy of either work.

sections.h: Baruch and the Letter in worship
sections.b:
Catholic. The Easter Vigil, the night before Easter, has the wisdom poem as its sixth reading (3:9–15, 32–4:4).

Orthodox. On the eve of the Nativity the Orthodox read 3:36–4:4 under the heading "Jeremiah (Baruch 3:35–4:4)". So on the eve of Christ's birth the church hears 3:38, the verse that Cyprian and the Apostolic Constitutions quote as "After this He was seen upon earth" and read of the incarnation. The heading itself shows the old habit of reading Baruch as part of Jeremiah.

Anglican. Article VI lists "Baruch the Prophet" among the books the Church reads "for example of life and instruction of manners."

Jewish. The Apostolic Constitutions (5.20), a Christian work, say that Jews in their day read Lamentations and Baruch when they gathered on the tenth day of Gorpiaeus, and they quote "This is our God" (3:36) as a prophecy of Christ that the Jews read unwillingly. C. H. Toy judged the report hardly authoritative, and true at most of some Greek-speaking Jewish group. The rabbis never counted the book (Bava Batra 14b lists the Prophets without it).

• Baruch son of Neriah. Jeremiah's scribe (Jeremiah 36:4; Jeremiah 45:1). In Jeremiah 43:6 he is taken to Egypt with Jeremiah. See the topic Baruch the Scribe.
  • Jeconiah. Jehoiachin, the king of Judah taken to Babylon in 597 BC (2 Kings 24:12–15).
  • Belshazzar. In Baruch, as in Daniel 5, the son of Nebuchadnezzar (1:11). In Babylonian records he is the son of Nabonidus; see the note at Daniel 5:2 for how readers explain "father" and "son."
  • The river Sud (1:4). Otherwise unknown. Whitehouse notes that the Syriac reads "river of Sur"; Toy suggested that Sud is a miswriting of Kebar, Ezekiel's river.
  • The Everlasting. In the mother's poem God is called by a title, "the Everlasting" (Greek ho aiōnios, 4:10 and often).
  • Wisdom, understanding, insight. The wisdom poem uses three Greek words, sophia, epistēmē and phronēsis, rendered the same way through the book.
  • The refrain. The Letter closes many rounds with a refrain: "This makes it plain that they are not gods. So have no fear of them" (6:14), with small changes each time.

spec.title: Claude's theory: Baruch's frame is modeled on his brother's scroll
spec.body: Jeremiah 51:59–64 tells how Seraiah son of Neriah, son of Mahseiah, went to Babylon with Zedekiah, carrying a scroll Jeremiah had written. He was told: "When you reach Babylon, take a look, and read all these words out loud" (Jeremiah 51:61), and then to tie a stone to it and throw it into the Euphrates. Jeremiah 32:12 gives Baruch the same father and grandfather, so Seraiah was Baruch's brother (Gigot also takes them as brothers). Baruch 1:1–4 tells a matching story: Baruch son of Neriah writes a book in Babylon and reads it aloud to the exiles by a river. The writer may have built his frame on that model, giving the scribe who never went to Babylon in Jeremiah's book the journey his brother made. This would explain why the frame insists on a public reading and names a river. This is my own suggestion; I did not find it in the sources I read, though commentators may have made it.

spec.title: Claude's theory: a service for a day of mourning
spec.body: The frame asks for the book to be read aloud in the Lord's house on feast days (1:14). The Apostolic Constitutions say Jews read Lamentations and Baruch together on the tenth of the month Gorpiaeus, which C. H. Toy took to be probably Ab. The Ninth of Ab is the day the Mishnah names for the destruction of the Temple, the first time and the second (Mishnah Taanit 4:6). The order of the book would fit a day of mourning: confession of the sins that brought the disaster (1:15–3:8), a reminder that the Law is still Israel's treasure (3:9–4:4), and comfort drawn from Isaiah 40 and 60 (4:5–5:9). If the book was used like this, its four pieces may have been gathered for one service, which would explain why such different writings were joined. This is my own theory, built on a Christian report that Toy doubted; nothing else ties Baruch to the Ninth of Ab.

prompts: Baruch reads the book by the river (1:3–4)

A scribe in a plain robe stands on a low rise by a slow river lined with willows, holding open a long scroll and reading aloud; around him sit and stand exiled men and women, a young king in a simple cloak among them, some weeping with their hands over their faces; behind them the brick towers of a great city fade into haze. Style: sketched by hand onto an old scroll, ink and faded earth colors, mixing ancient manuscript drawing with cave-painting figures and loose modern lines; soft torn edges, no hard border or rectangle.

A tall woman with a city wall and towers drawn as a crown on her head stands on a hilltop; on one side of her, in gray, she wears sackcloth and waves farewell to a line of children led away by soldiers; on the other side, in warm gold, she wears a shining robe and a high headdress and looks east, where the same children come back over leveled hills, carried high as if on thrones, under trees that lean over them for shade. Style: hand-drawn on an aged scroll, ink wash and gold leaf, part medieval manuscript, part cave drawing, part modern sketch; soft edges, no frame.

A street procession in ancient Babylon: priests carry wooden gods covered in gold and silver on their shoulders; the gods' faces are blackened with lamp smoke, a bat clings to one head, swallows circle another, and a cat sits on a shoulder; at the side of the street a small group of exiles watches, unafraid, one of them pointing and smiling. Style: sketched onto a scroll with brown ink and faded color, mixing Babylonian relief carving, cave-drawing figures and modern cartoon lines; soft edges, no hard rectangle.
The scarecrow in the cucumber field (6:69)

A small field of cucumber vines under a pale sky; in the middle a scarecrow made of a post and rags, painted with a gold face like a temple statue; crows sit unbothered on its arms and pick at the vines. Style: quick hand sketch on an old scroll, ink and watercolor, half ancient manuscript, half modern drawing; soft torn edges, no border.
reading: Sean A. Adams, Baruch and the Epistle of Jeremiah: A Commentary Based on the Texts in Codex Vaticanus (Brill, 2014)
A recent commentary on the Greek of both works, from the same manuscript this site translates; it reads the Greek largely without a presumed Hebrew original.
Carey A. Moore, Daniel, Esther and Jeremiah: The Additions (Anchor Bible 44, 1977)
A standard English commentary on Baruch and the Letter with the other additions.
O. C. Whitehouse, "I Baruch," and C. J. Ball, "Epistle of Jeremy," in R. H. Charles, ed., The Apocrypha and Pseudepigrapha of the Old Testament, vol. 1 (1913)
Old but thorough introductions and notes, now public domain; Whitehouse argues for a date after AD 70, Ball for a Hebrew Letter of about 300 BC.
Robert R. Harwell, The Principal Versions of Baruch (1915)
A short public-domain study of the Greek, Syriac and Latin, with the case for a Hebrew original and a date before 100 BC.
Joseph Ziegler, ed., Jeremias, Baruch, Threni, Epistula Jeremiae (Göttingen Septuagint 15)
The critical edition of the Greek, with every manuscript reading; for advanced study.

canon.summary: Baruch, with the Letter of Jeremiah as its chapter 6, is in the Old Testament of the Catholic Church. The Orthodox churches read Baruch and the Letter as two books, and the Ethiopian Orthodox Church counts Baruch too. Anglicans and Lutherans place them among the Apocrypha, read for example of life but not to establish doctrine. The Reformed and Baptist confessions do not count them as Scripture, and they are not in the Jewish Bible.
accepted_by: Scripture, one of the deuterocanonical books, with the Letter of Jeremiah as its sixth chapter. The Council of Trent (Session 4, 8 April 1546) listed "Jeremias, with Baruch" among the sacred and canonical books, and declared anathema anyone who does not receive these books "entire with all their parts" as they are in the old Latin Vulgate. The Catechism (120) names Baruch between Lamentations and Ezekiel, and Catholic Bibles count the Letter inside Baruch (Orthodox Study Bible). Jerome had left Baruch out of his translation from the Hebrew (see below); the Latin Baruch of the Vulgate is the older Latin version, later added to it (Whitehouse).

Scripture, in the Old Testament. The Orthodox Study Bible lists Baruch and the Epistle of Jeremiah as two books, with Jeremiah and Lamentations. The Orthodox Church in America's answer names "the Prophecy of Baruch" among the books "accepted by Orthodox Christianity as canonical scripture"; it does not mention the Letter. Worship reads Baruch under Jeremiah's name: the readings for the eve of the Nativity include "Jeremiah (Baruch 3:35–4:4)." The old Greek lists count both works inside Jeremiah. Athanasius (367) has "Jeremiah with Baruch, Lamentations, and the epistle, one book." Cyril of Jerusalem has "of Jeremiah one, including Baruch and Lamentations and the Epistle," and canon 60 of Laodicea, whose genuineness is doubted, has the same four. The Synod of Jerusalem (1672), in the Confession of Dositheus, takes as Scripture the books "collected from the Synod of Laodicea" and adds seven more; Baruch and the Letter are in that Laodicea list, and are not named among the seven. Philaret's catechism counts "of Jeremiah" among the 22 books and does not name Baruch; it says Sirach "and certain others" are left out of the count "because they do not exist in the Hebrew."

Scripture. Cowley's study of the canon lists Baruch among the books of the narrower count of the 81-book Bible. In the Ethiopic Bible Jeremiah 1–52 is followed by Baruch (five chapters, shorter than the Greek) and by a book of Jeremiah's lamentations. That book holds Lamentations 1–5, "the epistle to the captives" (the Letter) as its chapter 6, a prophecy against Pashhur, and the story known as 4 Baruch.
Other Oriental Orthodox churches (Coptic, Syriac, Armenian)

Read in their own ancient translations, all made from the Greek: Syriac (including the Syro-Hexapla of 616–617), a Coptic version from the Cairo codex of the Prophets and a Sahidic one that includes the Letter, and Armenian (Whitehouse). Ephrem the Syrian (300s) treated Baruch as Scripture (Whitehouse).

Among the Apocrypha. Article VI of the Thirty-Nine Articles names "Baruch the Prophet" among the other books which, "as Hierome saith," the church reads "for example of life and instruction of manners" but does not apply "to establish any doctrine." The Letter is not named separately; the King James Version (1611), made in the same church, prints it as Baruch's sixth chapter.

Among the Apocrypha. Luther's German Bible (quoted here from the Wittenberg edition of 1545) printed Baruch, with the Letter of Jeremiah attached to it, among the Apocrypha, under the heading Apocrypha: Das sind Bücher, so der heiligen Schrifft nicht gleich gehalten, vnd doch nützlich vnd gut zu lesen sind (books not held equal to Holy Scripture, and yet useful and good to read). In his preface to Baruch Luther called it a very slight book, said the number of years does not fit the histories, and wrote that he had nearly let it go with 3 and 4 Esdras (Salzmann).
Not Scripture. The Westminster Confession (1.3) says the books "commonly called Apocrypha" are not divinely inspired, are no part of the canon, and are of no authority in the church.
Not Scripture. The Second London Baptist Confession (1689, 1.3) repeats Westminster almost word for word: the Apocrypha "are of no authority to the church of God."

Not Scripture. The Talmud's order of the Prophets (Bava Batra 14b) has no Baruch, and Jerome says the Hebrews of his day neither read nor had it. A Christian work, the Apostolic Constitutions (about 380), says that Jews read Lamentations and Baruch on the tenth of Gorpiaeus; Toy thought this hardly authoritative, and true at most of some Greek-speaking group. He wrote that the Alexandrian Jews accepted the book "as a work of edification." Rabbinic tradition remembers Baruch himself as Ezra's teacher in Babylonia (Megillah 16b).

Widely used, usually as part of Jeremiah. Irenaeus (late 100s) quotes 4:36–5:9 as what "Jeremiah the prophet has pointed out," Cyprian quotes 3:36–38 under Jeremiah's name, and Hippolytus answers the followers of Noetus, who used the same verses (Whitehouse adds Athenagoras, Clement of Alexandria, Origen, Tertullian and Lactantius). Origen's list, as Eusebius gives it, has "Jeremiah, with Lamentations and the epistle in one," and does not name Baruch. Among the Fathers, Jerome alone set Baruch aside, because it was not in the Hebrew (Whitehouse).

provenance.h: When and where it was written
provenance.b:
The book gives its own date: the fifth year, on the seventh of a month it does not name, "the time when the Chaldeans captured Jerusalem and set it on fire" (1:2), so about 582 BC. Whitehouse noted that some (Fritzsche, Gifford) counted from the fall of 587–586 BC and others (Eichhorn, Kneucker) from the first capture of 597, when the Temple still stood, which would better fit the offerings of 1:10. C. H. Toy called the date "obscure": it may mean 581 BC or, more probably in his view, 592 BC, taken from Ezekiel's count from Jehoiachin's captivity.

Scholars who do not take the frame at face value have offered every period after that. Ewald put the prose at the end of the Persian empire. C. H. Toy (1902) thought the confession came after Daniel and that an editor of the Maccabean period joined it to the frame; he put the wisdom poem in the early Maccabean period. Harwell (1915) argued that the whole book was written before 100 BC and translated into Greek before the Christian era, and that the poems were probably older than the Maccabees. Thackeray had shown that the prose of Baruch 1–2 and the later chapters of Greek Jeremiah were translated by one hand; Harwell extended this to the whole book, on the ground that all of it was written in Hebrew. Kneucker, Schürer and Whitehouse (1913) read it after AD 70, with Nebuchadnezzar and Belshazzar standing for Vespasian and Titus; Whitehouse put the prose about AD 74. Gigot's Catholic Encyclopedia article answered that Catholics "easily disprove" so late a date. The latest possible date is fixed by Irenaeus, who quotes the book late in the 100s AD.

For the Letter, Ball (1913) argued from its "seven generations" (6:2) that it was written about 317–306 BC, among Babylonian Jews. Adams (2020) says that a Hebrew original, if it existed, was written between the 500s and the first century BC, and that the Greek came after Alexander, likely in the 200s or 100s BC. The place is unknown for both works.

No Hebrew text of either work survives, and the evidence is indirect.

  • Hebraisms. The Greek of 1:1–3:8 reads like translation: Whitehouse lists words such as manna for the grain offering (1:10) and Hebrew-style relative clauses (2:4; 2:26), and in 1913 he wrote that nearly all living scholars held the prose was composed in Hebrew. The wisdom poem was argued both ways; Whitehouse thought the mother's poem was Greek from the start, while his editor R. H. Charles found a Hebraism in 5:6 and argued for Hebrew. Harwell (1915) argued for Hebrew throughout.
  • Origen's marks. The Syro-Hexapla, a Syriac translation of Origen's Greek made in 616–617, has a note at the end saying the whole book was under the obelus, Origen's sign for what is not in the Hebrew. Yet in the margin at 1:17 and 2:3 it notes three times "not found in the Hebrew," and it marks one clause in 2:1 with an asterisk. Whitehouse held that the notes at 1:17 and 2:3 make a Hebrew original of the prose "fairly certain," and Gigot also cited them for a Hebrew original; Nestle and Harwell argued that they refer to the passages Baruch borrows (Daniel 9:8 and the curse of eating one's children), not to a Hebrew Baruch.
  • Theodotion. The Syro-Hexapla's margin gives five readings marked as Theodotion's (Harwell). Gigot thought it "highly probable" that Theodotion translated Baruch from Hebrew; Harwell thought Theodotion revised the Greek.
  • Jerome says only that the Hebrews neither read nor have the book.
  • The Letter. Ball and most scholars of the 1900s argued for a Hebrew original, explaining odd Greek phrases as misread Hebrew ("marble" and "linen" in 6:71 are one example). Fritzsche and Schürer in the 1800s, and Benjamin Wright and Sean Adams more recently, read it as Greek composition (Adams). VanderKam also takes Greek as "apparently the original language."

The Greek is in Codex Vaticanus (300s AD), which Swete prints and this site translates, in Alexandrinus (400s), Marchalianus (500s) and Venetus, and in later minuscules; Sinaiticus has neither work (Whitehouse); Adams thinks both were in a part of the codex now lost in a gap after Lamentations 2:20, since in Sinaiticus Lamentations follows Jeremiah directly. For the Letter, Adams judges Vaticanus the best text, with few and minor differences among the codices. A papyrus fragment from Qumran Cave 7, 7Q2, all of whose legible fragments are Greek (VanderKam), is thought to hold Letter 43–44 in a form close to the later Lucianic Greek, but has only twenty-two letters (Adams). Nothing of Baruch 1–5 has been found at Qumran (VanderKam).

The ancient translations were all made from the Greek: Syriac (an ordinary version and the Syro-Hexapla), two Old Latin versions (one of which became the Vulgate's Baruch), Arabic, Ethiopic, Coptic and Armenian (Whitehouse; Harwell). Jerome did not translate either work, and the oldest Vulgate manuscript, Codex Amiatinus, does not have them (Whitehouse).

provenance.h: What it builds on in the Hebrew Bible
provenance.b:
Both works are made largely of earlier Scripture, and the links run from the Hebrew Bible to Baruch.

  • Daniel 9:4–19: whole clauses of the confession (1:15–2:19).
  • Jeremiah: the call to serve the king of Babylon (2:21–23; Jeremiah 27:11–12), the silenced voices of joy (2:23; Jeremiah 7:34), the everlasting covenant (2:35; Jeremiah 32:40); the Letter builds on Jeremiah 10:1–16 and Jeremiah 29.
  • Deuteronomy 28–32: the curses, eating one's children (2:3), the nation from far away (4:15), the return (2:29–35), and the sacrifice "to demons, not to God" (4:7; Deuteronomy 32:17).
  • Job 28, Proverbs 8 and Deuteronomy 30:12–13: the search for wisdom (3:15–31).
  • Isaiah 40–66: the comfort of Jerusalem, the leveled hills and the children carried home (4:36–5:9; Isaiah 40:4; Isaiah 60:4).
  • Psalm 115 and Isaiah 44:9–20: idols that cannot see, speak or save (chapter 6).

It also has close links outside the Hebrew Bible: Sirach 24 in the wisdom poem, Psalms of Solomon 11 in the last verses, and 2 Maccabees 2:1–3 with the Letter.

rejected_why.h: It is not in the Jewish Bible
rejected_why.b: The Jewish Bible's Prophets are Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Isaiah and the Twelve (Bava Batra 14b); Baruch is not among them, and no Hebrew copy of it or of the Letter survives. The Westminster Confession lists the 39 books of the Hebrew Bible as the Old Testament, with no Baruch (1.2), and gives the others no authority (1.3). Philaret's Orthodox catechism also counts 22 books and leaves Sirach "and certain others" out of the count "because they do not exist in the Hebrew."

Jerome, in the preface to his translation of Jeremiah from the Hebrew, wrote that he had left out the book of Baruch, Jeremiah's scribe, which the Hebrews neither read nor have, and that he expected curses from the jealous for it. The preface says nothing about the Letter. Elsewhere, Gigot reports, Jerome called the Letter pseudepigraphos, a writing under a false name. His Latin Bible had neither work; the Vulgate's Baruch is the Old Latin, added later (Whitehouse). Article VI cites him ("as Hierome saith") for its rule that these books are read for example of life, not to establish doctrine.

Origen's list of the 22 books of the Jews, as Eusebius reports it, has "Jeremiah, with Lamentations and the epistle in one," and leaves Baruch out, though Origen quoted Baruch elsewhere (Whitehouse). The note at the end of the Syro-Hexapla that the whole book was under the obelus (Harwell) shows that Origen found no Hebrew text to set beside it.

The Reformers' general case against the Apocrypha applies here: these books are not in the Hebrew canon, and the church may not make doctrine from them (Westminster Confession 1.3; Article VI). Anglicans and Lutherans kept Baruch for reading. Against Baruch in particular, Luther's preface counted it a very slight book and objected that its count of the years does not agree with the histories (Salzmann). Whitehouse noted that among Protestant German scholars until Ewald there was a tendency to think little of the book.

Whitehouse and Toy note points in 1:1–14 that are hard to fit with the history in Kings and Jeremiah, and Gigot, writing for Catholics, grants that "serious difficulties" have been raised:

  • Baruch in Babylon. Jeremiah's book last shows Baruch taken to Egypt: "They also took Jeremiah the prophet and Baruch son of Neriah" (Jeremiah 43:6), and they went as far as Tahpanhes (Jeremiah 43:7). Nothing in the Bible takes him to Babylon. Whitehouse noted that this silence proves little.
  • Belshazzar as Nebuchadnezzar's son (1:11–12), as in Daniel 5, though Babylonian records make him the son of Nabonidus.
  • Sacrifice in a burned Temple. The exiles send money for burnt offerings and incense on the altar (1:10) after the city and house were burned (1:2).
  • Joakim son of Hilkiah, son of Shallum (1:7). The Greek calls him "the priest" (the KJV says "the high priest"). 1 Chronicles 6:13 does have "Shallum fathered Hilkiah," but the line goes on "Hilkiah fathered Azariah," not Joakim, and the head priest in 586 BC was Seraiah (2 Kings 25:18). A Joiakim of the same line, grandson of Jozadak, appears only after the return (Nehemiah 12:10, 26).
  • The vessels (1:8): silver vessels said to have been made by Zedekiah and sent back, which the history books do not mention.
  • The Letter's "seven generations" (6:2) instead of Jeremiah's seventy years (Jeremiah 29:10).

rejected_why.h: How the churches that keep it answer
rejected_why.b:
On the canon. Baruch was read as part of Jeremiah from the 100s on: Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria and Cyprian quote it under his name (Harwell). The Greek lists of Athanasius, Cyril and Laodicea counted Baruch and the Letter inside the canon even when they set other books outside it (Whitehouse). Gigot held that a study of the canon shows the book has as much right to be held inspired as any other, and that Trent defined it "sacred and canonical."

On Baruch in Babylon. Whitehouse noted that Jeremiah's book says nothing of Baruch after Egypt, so a later journey cannot be ruled out. A rabbinic tradition places Baruch in Babylonia, where Ezra stayed with him as his disciple for as long as Baruch lived (Megillah 16b). Another tradition, which Jerome preserved, has Baruch and Jeremiah both die in Egypt; Gigot notes that it conflicts with Baruch 1.

On the dates and names. For "father" and "son," defenders of Daniel give the same answers here (see the note at Daniel 5:2). For the offerings, Jeremiah 41:5 shows men bringing "grain offerings and frankincense" to the house of the LORD after the Temple was burned, so some worship went on at the site (Whitehouse). Counting the fifth year from 597, when the Temple still stood, also removes the problem (Eichhorn, Kneucker), though Whitehouse notes that this goes against the words of 1:2. Gigot wrote that Catholic answers are considered sufficient by Catholic scholars generally.

On the kind of book. Catholic teaching since the Second Vatican Council says that truth "is set forth and expressed differently in texts which are variously historical, prophetic, poetic" and so on, and that Scripture teaches "that truth which God wanted put into sacred writings for the sake of salvation" (Dei Verbum 11–12). Applying that teaching here is my own step (Claude's), not a church's: no church text I read applies it to Baruch. On it, a Catholic reader could take the frame of Baruch and the title of the Letter as a literary setting rather than a historical report without denying that the books are inspired. Gigot argued in 1907 that if an inspired editor joined the parts, the book remains inspired.

cited_in.b: Paul applies Deuteronomy 30:12–14 to Christ: "Who will go up into heaven?" (Romans 10:6). Baruch applies the same verses to wisdom: who climbed up into the sky and took her, who crossed to the far side of the sea and found her (3:29–30). Both reuse Deuteronomy for something God gives that no one could fetch. Paul's "abyss" (Romans 10:7) is in neither Deuteronomy nor Baruch, and his words follow Deuteronomy, not Baruch, so there is no sign that he used Baruch; the link is a shared way of reading Deuteronomy 30.

"The Word became flesh and pitched his tent among us" (John 1:14). Cyprian, Hippolytus and the Apostolic Constitutions read 3:38 as a prophecy of this; Cyprian quotes it as "After this He was seen upon earth, and He conversed with men" to prove that Christ is God, and Origen cites it too (Whitehouse). The Greek verbs have no subject word and no gender. Whitehouse judged that the subject is "probably God as in verse 36, but it might be wisdom"; the Syriac, the Latin and the Arabic read "he" (Whitehouse), as the KJV does. The Plain English Translation follows the subject of 3:36–37: "After this he was seen on earth and went about among human beings" (3:38). Others read it of wisdom given to Israel as the Law: Gigot wrote that "only in the guise of the Law has Wisdom appeared on the earth," and the New American Bible prints "Thus she has appeared on earth." There is no shared wording in the Greek (John's eskēnōsen, Baruch's synanestraphē); John's "pitched his tent" is closer to Sirach 24:8, where wisdom pitches her tent in Jacob. Toy judged 3:38 "undoubtedly a Christian interpolation," and Whitehouse names earlier scholars who suspected a Christian gloss (Grotius, Hitzig, Hilgenfeld, Kneucker, Rothstein); but both Hippolytus and the followers of Noetus he answered quoted it in the early 200s. So the link is a reading of the verse, not a quotation; the churches' readings stand side by side on the card for chapter 3.

"What they sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God" (1 Corinthians 10:20). Baruch's "offering sacrifices to demons and not to God" (4:7) and Paul's share the same words, but both come from Deuteronomy 32:17, "They offered sacrifices to demons, not to God," in its Greek form, which Baruch follows closely (Whitehouse). A shared source, not a quotation of Baruch.

Survivors who would not give up "idols of gold, silver, bronze, stone, and wood, which are not able to see or hear or walk" (Revelation 9:20). The Letter mocks "silver gods, gold gods and wooden gods" (6:3) that cannot see, help or save. Revelation's list of metals and of what idols cannot do is closer to Daniel 5:23 and Psalm 115:4–7, so this is the common Jewish satire on idols, not a use of the Letter.

"Many will come from the sunrise and the sunset" (Matthew 8:11). Baruch pictures Jerusalem's children gathered from east and west (4:37; 5:5). Both draw on Isaiah's promise of a gathering from the sunrise and the sunset (Isaiah 43:5); there is no sign of direct dependence.

Jesus says "nobody has gone up into heaven except the one who came down out of heaven" (John 3:13). Baruch asks who went up into heaven to bring wisdom down (3:29), as Proverbs 30:4 asks who climbed up to heaven and came back down. A shared biblical question; Christian readers have answered it with Christ, but John does not cite Baruch.

reliability.verdict: This is Claude's analysis, not a church's judgment. As a witness to Jewish prayer and hope in the centuries around Jesus, Baruch is valuable: it shows how Jews confessed the nation's sins in the words of Daniel and Deuteronomy, joined wisdom to the Law, and gave Jerusalem a mother's voice; the Letter shows how Jews mocked the gods of their neighbors. Its date is unknown, which limits what it can prove about any one time. As a text, the Greek is well preserved in the great codices, but no Hebrew survives, and the oldest physical trace is a scrap of twenty-two letters that may be the Letter. As history, the frame's details do not fit the history of Kings and Jeremiah, and critical scholars from Toy and Whitehouse on read Baruch's name and Jeremiah's as literary settings. Catholic scholars such as Gigot answered the difficulties one by one, and Catholic teaching on literary forms leaves room to read the frame as a setting. Measured by the 66 books, Baruch mostly repeats and applies them; it goes beyond them in identifying wisdom with the Law and in its picture of Jerusalem's return, and it does not conflict with them in doctrine.

sections.h: 1. A witness to Jewish faith before and around Jesus: high
sections.b: Even on the latest proposed date, Baruch shows a Judaism that prays in the words of Scripture and answers disaster with confession: "Righteousness belongs to the Lord our God, but to us belongs the shame of our faces" (1:15; compare Daniel 9:7). It shows the joining of wisdom and Torah (4:1) also found in Sirach 24, and the hope for a gathering of all Israel from east and west (4:37; 5:5) also found in the Psalms of Solomon. The Letter shows how a Jewish preacher answered the pull of a great empire's worship with satire and a simple rule: do not fear them. A Christian source says Jews read Baruch with Lamentations (Apostolic Constitutions 5.20), but Toy judged that report hardly authoritative, so its use in Jewish worship is uncertain. Its value is limited by its uncertain date: it cannot be used to show what Jews believed in one century rather than another.

The Greek of both works is in the great codices from the 300s on, and Adams finds few and minor differences among them for the Letter. Swete's apparatus and the versions show more variation in Baruch 1–5. No Hebrew text survives of either work, so every claim about an original Hebrew is reconstruction, and the Syro-Hexapla's notes "not found in the Hebrew" may refer to the passages Baruch borrows rather than to a Hebrew Baruch (Harwell). The Qumran fragment 7Q2, if it is the Letter, is the earliest evidence that the Greek Letter existed and gives a firm latest date for it (Adams); nothing of Baruch 1–5 was found at Qumran (VanderKam). The Latin, Syriac, Coptic, Ethiopic, Arabic and Armenian translations were all made from the Greek.

Baruch presents itself as written by Baruch in Babylon about 582 BC; the Letter, as a letter of Jeremiah to the captives. The evidence makes both claims hard to hold as history: Jeremiah 43:6 last shows Baruch in Egypt; Belshazzar is called Nebuchadnezzar's son (1:11), as in Daniel; offerings are sent to a burned Temple (1:2; 1:10); the priest Joakim (1:7) is not in the priestly lists; the confession borrows from Daniel, which Toy held rules out Baruch as its writer; and the Letter's "seven generations" (6:2) do not match Jeremiah's seventy years. There are answers: Baruch's later life is unknown, and rabbinic tradition puts him in Babylon (Megillah 16b); "son" can mean successor; worship went on at the Temple's site (Jeremiah 41:5); the fifth year may be counted from 597. Taken together, the case against reading the frame as history is strong in my judgment, and Toy wrote in 1902 that "very few scholars" still held that Baruch wrote the book. The Catholic Church teaches that the truth of a book is to be read according to its literary form (Dei Verbum 12), so in my judgment this does not settle whether it is inspired; no church text applies that teaching to Baruch. The Letter's details about Babylonian worship, by contrast, fit what is known of Babylonian religion (Ball).

sections.h: 4. Agreement with the 66 books, point by point
sections.b:
• Agrees: God's justice in punishing Israel's sin (1:15–2:10; Daniel 9:7; Deuteronomy 28); his mercy for his own sake and his name's (2:14; 3:5; Daniel 9:18–19); the promise of return after repentance (2:29–35; Deuteronomy 30:1–5; Jeremiah 32:37–41); wisdom as God's gift that no human can fetch (3:15–31; Job 28:12–28); Jerusalem as a bereaved mother comforted by God (4:5–5:9; Lamentations 1; Isaiah 54; Isaiah 60); idols as helpless wood and metal (chapter 6; Psalm 115:4–8; Isaiah 44:9–20; Jeremiah 10:1–16); praying for the rulers of the land of exile (1:11; Jeremiah 29:7).
  • Goes beyond: (a) wisdom is the Law: "the book of the commands of God" (4:1), said more plainly than in Proverbs, close to Sirach 24; (b) 3:38, which Cyprian, the Apostolic Constitutions and Orthodox worship take as a prophecy of the incarnation (John 1:14), while Gigot and the New American Bible read it of wisdom in the Law and Toy as a later addition; (c) demons as the receivers of pagan sacrifice and the dwellers of ruined cities (4:7, 35), as in Deuteronomy 32:17 and Isaiah 13:21, but more developed; (d) seven generations of exile (6:2), a different count from Jeremiah 29:10.
  • Differs or may conflict: no point of doctrine is in conflict with the 66 books. The historical frame differs from Jeremiah 43 (Baruch in Egypt), and the seven generations differ from the seventy years. Luther counted the mismatch of the years against Baruch (Salzmann); Gigot held that the Catholic answers to the historical difficulties are sufficient.

how_to_read.b: Remember who counts it as Scripture. If you are Catholic or Orthodox, Baruch and the Letter are in your Bible, and your church's teaching and worship are your guide to them. If you are Protestant, they are not Scripture for you, though Anglican and Lutheran tradition commends them for example of life. For each church's answer side by side, see Jeremiah's book page, "Are Baruch and the Letter of Jeremiah part of the Bible?"

how_to_read.h: Read it as four pieces and a letter
how_to_read.b: Read the frame (1:1–14), the confession (1:15–3:8), the wisdom poem (3:9–4:4) and the mother's poem (4:5–5:9) one at a time, and ask who is speaking and to whom. Then read chapter 6 as its own work. The chapter pages give each piece its own card on who it was for.

Read Daniel 9:4–19 next to 1:15–2:19, Deuteronomy 28–30 next to 2:20–35, Job 28 and Deuteronomy 30:11–14 next to 3:9–4:4, Lamentations 1 and Isaiah 40, 54 and 60 next to 4:5–5:9, and Jeremiah 10:1–16 and Jeremiah 29 next to chapter 6. You will see how much of the book is Scripture rearranged, and where it adds its own voice.

On the frame's history, on 3:38 and on the Letter's seven generations, the churches and scholars give real answers, set out above and on the chapter pages. Read each in its strongest form before deciding.

how_to_read.h: Using it in study or teaching
how_to_read.b: When you quote it, say what it is: "Baruch, in the Old Testament of Catholic and Orthodox Christians and among the Apocrypha for Protestants." Say which numbering you use, since the King James Version numbers some verses one lower (see "About this translation"). It is a good background for how Jews prayed in exile, for wisdom and Law in the New Testament, and for Paul's and Revelation's words about idols.
